questions.question: Which red-eye presentation needs urgent ophthalmic/emergency assessment rather than routine conjunctivitis treatment?
choices: Bilateral itching with watery discharge and preserved vision
Unilateral eye pain, photophobia, and reduced visual acuity in a contact-lens wearer
Mild transient redness after crying
Stable dry-eye symptoms that improve with lubricants
questions.explanation: Pain, photophobia, reduced acuity, and contact-lens exposure raise concern for corneal disease or another urgent eye condition. Do not anchor on conjunctivitis.

questions.question: What is an essential functional assessment for most eye complaints?
choices: Visual acuity in each eye when feasible
Only blood pressure
A routine CT scan
Skin-patch testing
questions.explanation: Visual acuity documents function and helps identify vision-threatening presentations. It should be obtained early when feasible without delaying emergency care.

questions.question: A patient reports many new floaters, flashes, and a gray curtain over part of one eye. What is the safest response?
choices: Reassure because the eye is painless
Arrange urgent ophthalmic assessment for possible retinal tear/detachment
Treat as allergic conjunctivitis
Wait until the next annual vision screening
questions.explanation: New significant flashes/floaters with shadow or curtain can indicate retinal tear or detachment and needs urgent assessment.

questions.question: What is the priority after a chemical eye exposure?
choices: Complete a detailed outpatient history before acting
Immediate irrigation and emergency ophthalmic assessment according to local protocol
Patch the eye and schedule follow-up next week
Perform routine hearing screening
questions.explanation: Chemical eye exposure is time-sensitive. Begin decontamination immediately and escalate; do not delay for a prolonged office workup.

questions.question: Which hearing complaint requires prompt evaluation?
choices: Gradual symmetric hearing change over years
Sudden unilateral hearing loss with tinnitus or dizziness
A brief ear pop during an elevator ride that resolves
Stable mild itching of the outer ear
questions.explanation: Sudden hearing loss needs prompt evaluation and audiometric/specialty pathway access. It should not automatically be attributed to wax or congestion.

questions.question: Which throat presentation is most concerning for airway compromise or deep-neck infection?
choices: Mild sore throat with improving rhinorrhea
Drooling, muffled voice, difficulty swallowing, neck swelling, and fever
Brief scratchy throat after speaking loudly
Mild stable hoarseness after a concert
questions.explanation: Drooling, dysphagia, muffled voice, neck swelling, fever, toxicity, or breathing difficulty requires urgent airway-focused assessment.

questions.question: Why should sudden painless monocular vision loss be treated as an emergency until evaluated?
choices: Painless symptoms cannot be serious
It may represent a time-sensitive ocular or vascular process
It is always a refractive error
It can be managed only with lubricating drops
questions.explanation: Sudden monocular vision loss can result from serious ocular or vascular disease. Urgent evaluation is required.

questions.question: What is the safest principle for a suspected penetrating eye injury?
choices: Apply firm pressure over the eye
Avoid pressure on the globe and arrange emergency care
Remove any embedded object in clinic
Delay referral until redness subsides
questions.explanation: Suspected globe injury is an emergency. Protect the eye, avoid pressure/manipulation, and use the emergency ophthalmic pathway.

questions.question: Which oral finding merits an appropriate expedited referral pathway?
choices: A small traumatic ulcer that heals promptly
Persistent unexplained ulceration or a bleeding, nonhealing oral lesion
Brief dry mouth after exercise
A resolved minor lip bite
questions.explanation: Persistent, unexplained, bleeding, nonhealing, or high-risk oral lesions require reassessment and dental/ENT/oral-medicine referral as appropriate.

questions.question: What is essential to a safe outpatient eye, ENT, or oral plan?
choices: A vague instruction to return if symptoms are annoying
Document function/laterality, give explicit vision/airway/neurologic precautions, and ensure referral or result ownership
Assume a normal initial appearance excludes deterioration
Avoid recording examination limits
questions.explanation: Clear safety-netting and closed-loop follow-up are essential because vision, airway, and infectious conditions can change quickly.
